                                   PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                      §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                   §
STANDARDS                                    §                    OF TEXAS

                  COMMENTS OF MCADAMS ENERGY GROUP ON
                   STAFF’S RECOMMENDED ADOPTION ORDER


Introduction

McAdams Energy Group is a full-service consulting ﬁrm assisting a variety of large loads
seeking electricity services from the grid administered by the Electric Reliability Council of
Texas (ERCOT). We appreciate and commend Commission Staff’s effort to create a system
of validation measures through Project 58481 to ensure that large loads seeking grid service
are not speculative or transient consistent with the intent of SB 6.

It is important to remember that SB 6 was intended to protect existing customers from
stranded infrastructure costs while also supporting continued business development in
Texas. The Recommended Adoption Order should preserve both objectives. As written,
however, the ﬁnancial security provisions could create substantial uncertainty and
potentially deter large load investment in Texas. We therefore request that the
Commission provide clarifying language in the ﬁnal adopted order and conﬁrm whether the
attached ﬂow diagram accurately reﬂects the intended operation of the rule.



SLLIA security requirement creates potentially unbounded ﬁnancial exposure

Under the recommended rule, a large load customer must post ﬁnancial security when the
SLLIA is executed equal to the greater of:

   1.   $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand; or

   2.   the customer’s allocated system upgrade costs from the applicable interconnection
        study.

The second prong creates signiﬁcant uncertainty because the rule does not clearly deﬁne
what costs may be included in “allocated system upgrade costs” or establish an express
limit on that exposure. Depending on the outcome of the interconnection study, the required
security could vary substantially from project to project and could become very large. While
the Commission has been clear that cost allocation will be addressed in separate


                                              1
 rulemaking proceedings under Project Nos. 58000 and 58484, the allocation of costs does
little to address the uncertainty of high costs for system upgrades.

For projects assigned signiﬁcant transmission upgrades, those collateral requirements
could become so large and so difficult to predict, that some customers may choose not to
enter the ERCOT interconnection process at all. Customers may instead pursue fully
islanded conﬁgurations or locate projects in jurisdictions with more predictable ﬁnancial
requirements.

This concern is not limited to data centers. The same requirements apply to manufacturing
facilities and other large industrial projects considering whether to invest or expand in Texas.
The ﬁnancial framework intended to protect against stranded costs could inadvertently
discourage otherwise viable projects from connecting to the ERCOT system, resulting in an
unintended and inequitable distribution of transmission costs to ratepayers.



Requested Commission clariﬁcation

We request that the Commission clarify the following in the ﬁnal adopted order:

   1. What costs are included in “allocated system upgrade costs,” how those costs are
      assigned, and whether any limits apply.

   2. Whether a customer’s allocated system upgrade costs and associated security
      requirement are ﬁxed at Standard Large Load Interconnection Agreement (SLLIA)
      execution or may increase if other projects withdraw or study assumptions change.
      As it stands now, the proposed text of §25.194 does not appear to address whether a
      customer's allocated security obligation remains locked if higher-queued or batch-
      mate projects withdraw during reﬁnement studies or construction.

   3. What speciﬁc risk additional security related to the large load minimum billing
      demand is intended to cover, and how that risk differs from the risk already secured
      through SLLIA ﬁnancial security.

   4. Whether existing SLLIA ﬁnancial security will be credited against any additional
      minimum billing demand related security so that customers are not required to
      collateralize the same exposure twice.

   5. Whether the security requirement is intended to reﬂect the full estimated cost of
      allocated system upgrades at SLLIA execution, or instead the costs that the
      transmission provider has actually incurred or become irrevocably committed to
      incur.

                                               2
 Conclusion

SB 6 sought to ensure that large loads bear an appropriate share of the costs associated with
their interconnection, but it did not displace the long-standing requirement in PURA
§36.003(b) that “a rate may not be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory
but must be sufficient, equitable, and consistent in application to each class of consumer.”
The Recommended Adoption Order reﬂects the Commission’s effort to reconcile that
requirement with the new principle in PURA §35.004(c-1), which seeks to ensure that a large
load contributes to its interconnection costs.

The remaining concern is the uncertainty around how broadly the Commission intends to
deﬁne the “costs to interconnect the large load.” The draft rule clearly seeks to go beyond
direct interconnection costs by allowing direct assignment, through either security
requirements or rates, of system upgrade costs associated with broader portions of the grid
that beneﬁt multiple customer classes.

Greater clarity is therefore necessary both to protect existing customers from stranded costs
and to provide large load customers with a predictable framework for ﬁnancing and
investment. Clear structure around the costs that may be assigned to large loads will help
ensure that the ﬁnal rule is consistent with SB 6, longstanding ratemaking principles, and
Texas’s broader interest in continued economic development.

                                                         Will McAdams

                                                         McAdams Energy Group, LLC
